case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, SC Appeal No. 104/99, decided on 3 October 2000

clause.text: Any accused person has the right to a fair trial and legal representation.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the appellant's right to a fair trial under Article 13(3) was violated due to failure to disclose a purported 9:30 p.m. statement by the sole eyewitness, Senaratne, and whether the credibility of the eyewitness evidence was sufficient to sustain conviction.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The appellant argued that the failure to produce the 9:30 p.m. statement impaired his right to a fair trial under Article 13(3), and that the sole eyewitness's evidence was unreliable and raised reasonable doubt about his guilt.
case_context.respondent_argument: The prosecution relied on the 11:30 p.m. statement as the first information and maintained the credibility of the eyewitness's testimony as accepted by the trial judge and affirmed by the Court of Appeal.
key_facts: The appellant was convicted of culpable homicide not amounting to murder based solely on the testimony of Senaratne, the deceased's father and sole eyewitness.
Senaratne claimed to have made a statement at 9:30 p.m. at the hospital police post, which was not produced or disclosed to the defense or court.
The prosecution sought to rely on a later 11:30 p.m. statement to police, which was disallowed as first information.
The Court of Appeal affirmed the conviction without adequately scrutinizing the eyewitness's credibility or the non-disclosure of the 9:30 p.m. statement.
The Supreme Court found serious doubts about the eyewitness's credibility and held that non-disclosure of the 9:30 p.m. statement violated the appellant's right to a fair trial.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that Article 13(3) guarantees not only legal representation but also a fair trial, which includes the right to receive all material information necessary for defense, such as witness statements. Failure to disclose the purported 9:30 p.m. statement constituted a violation of this right. The Court emphasized that the right to a fair trial encompasses the ancillary right to information necessary to prepare a defense. The Court also scrutinized the eyewitness's testimony closely and found it riddled with inconsistencies and doubts, warranting the benefit of the doubt to the accused.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found that either the 9:30 p.m. statement was never made, undermining the witness's credibility, or it was made but withheld, violating disclosure obligations and the right to a fair trial. The lack of corroboration and the suspicious nature of the eyewitness's evidence led the Court to conclude that the conviction could not stand. The Court set aside the conviction and acquitted the appellant.
principles_established: The right to a fair trial under Article 13(3) includes the right to disclosure of all material witness statements, whether or not the prosecution intends to use them.
Non-disclosure of material evidence that could impeach witness credibility amounts to a violation of the right to a fair trial.
An appellate court must closely scrutinize the evidence of a sole eyewitness, especially when doubts arise, and give the benefit of the doubt to the accused if reasonable.
The prosecution's duty to disclose is ongoing and includes statements made before trial.
The quality of evidence is more important than quantity; corroboration is necessary when the sole eyewitness's testimony is suspicious.
precedents_cited: Phato v. A.G. (1994) 3 Law Reports of the Commonwealth 506
R. v. Stinchcombe (1992) Law Reports of the Commonwealth (Crim) 68
Jagathsena and Others v. G.D.D. Perera, Inspector - Criminal Investigation Department and Mrs. Bandaranaike (1992) 1 SRI LR 371 at 380

outcome.holding: The appeal was allowed on the ground that the failure to disclose the 9:30 p.m. statement violated the appellant's right to a fair trial under Article 13(3). The conviction and sentence were set aside and the appellant was acquitted.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Conviction and sentence set aside; appellant acquitted.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 13(3) was central to the Court's reasoning because the appellant's claim of denial of a fair trial hinged on the non-disclosure of material evidence, which impaired his ability to defend himself. The Court's holding directly enforced the protections guaranteed by this clause.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court found that if the 9:30 p.m. statement existed, its non-disclosure to the defense and the Court violated Article 13(3). The eyewitness's credibility was seriously questioned due to inconsistencies and failure to produce this statement, leading to the conclusion that the appellant's right to a fair trial was impaired.
